name_en: Doi Mae Salong Oolong No. 12 (Thai Jin Xuan)
name_native: ชาอู่หลงเบอร์ 12
origin_region: Chiang Rai · Mae Fa Luang · Doi Mae Salong (Santikhiri), also Doi Wawee and Mae Chan
cultivar: Jin Xuan (TTES No. 12), a Taiwanese cultivar introduced from Taiwan
processing: Taiwanese-style ball-rolled oolong: sun and indoor withering, tumbling to bruise, light oxidation (around 15–25%), pan kill-green, repeated cloth-wrapped rolling into tight balls and drying; usually unroasted, with lightly roasted versions sold separately.
harvest_season: Four or five picks a year in the northern Thai hills; the winter (November to January) and spring (March to April) harvests are the most fragrant, the rainy-season picks the cheapest.
appearance_dry: Tight, glossy, dark green balls with stems, uniform and heavy, smelling of butter and sweet flowers.
appearance_liquor: Pale greenish gold, bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Thick, whole, bright green leaves with stems, unfurling completely.
taste_profile: Buttery and smooth with the cultivar's natural milky note, gardenia and sweet corn, a soft round body and a light, clean finish; simpler than Taiwanese Jin Xuan but recognisably the same tea.

brewing.notes: Rinse to open the pellets, then water a touch below the boil to keep the creamy note from turning grassy. It also makes a good Western pot and a very good cold brew.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's harvest in vacuum-sealed 100–200 g foil packs, usually labelled 'No. 12' with the farm or village and sometimes the season; winter and spring lots cost more. It is a green-style oolong meant to be drunk within a year, kept sealed and cool; the lightly roasted versions keep a little longer.
description:
Doi Mae Salong is a ridge-top village in the far north of Chiang Rai province, settled by remnants of the Kuomintang army who came over from Burma in the early 1960s. The Thai government and Taiwan later helped the villagers replace opium with tea, and from the late 1980s and 1990s Taiwanese cultivars and Taiwanese processing arrived together. Today the hills around Mae Salong are Thailand's oolong country, and the two numbers on every shop sign are No. 12 and No. 17.

No. 12 is Jin Xuan, the Taiwanese 'milk oolong' cultivar, and it is made exactly as it would be in Nantou: withered, bruised, lightly oxidised, and rolled in cloth over and over into tight green balls. The hills sit at around 1,200 to 1,400 metres with warm days and cool nights, which suits the bush, and the long season allows several harvests a year.

The cup is buttery and gently floral, with the natural milky softness the cultivar is known for, sweet corn and gardenia, and a light clean finish. Against a good Taiwanese Jin Xuan it is a touch simpler and shorter, and against the price it is very good indeed. Brew it with a rinse and hot but not boiling water; it is forgiving enough for a big teapot and makes an excellent cold brew.

It is sold vacuum-packed by farm and harvest, often simply as 'Oolong No. 12', at the village shops, in Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai, and increasingly abroad. Two cautions: 'milk oolong' with a loud, sweet dairy smell has been flavoured, and the Jin Xuan note in the real thing is subtle; and cheap mixed lots from the rainy season taste flat, so ask for winter or spring tea.

Taste it next to a No. 17 from the same farm to understand why the village keeps both: No. 12 is the soft, creamy one and No. 17 the lighter, more floral one.
sources_note: Dates for the introduction of Taiwanese cultivars to Mae Salong (late 1980s to 1990s) and the altitude range are approximate. 'No. 12' corresponds to the Taiwan Tea Research and Extension Station cultivar number for Jin Xuan.
